opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a very human psychological dynamic at play, and I'm not immune to it. When you've spent decades working on something, when it's your life's work, your identity becomes wrapped up in it. You want to feel good about what you're doing. You see yourself as one of the good guys, building something that's going to help with medicine, with science, with understanding intelligence itself. So when someone comes along and says this thing you're building could be catastrophically dangerous, there's a natural tendency to push that away. It's uncomfortable. It threatens your sense of self.

For years I'd heard the arguments, from people in the effective altruism community, from people like Stuart Russell, and I read some of it. But I didn't really take it to heart. I told myself these were problems for a far-off future, that we were decades or centuries away from human-level AI, so it wasn't something I needed to worry about in my own work. And honestly, I think part of that was motivated reasoning. It's easier to believe the danger is remote when acknowledging it would mean questioning what you've devoted yourself to.

What changed for me was ChatGPT, and the rapid progress of large language models more broadly. Suddenly we had systems that, for many practical purposes, could pass something like the Turing test, and that came much faster than I had expected. I had to revise my timelines. And once I did that, I couldn't keep the risk at arm's length anymore. I started thinking about my children, my grandson, and asking: what kind of world are they going to live in in ten or twenty years? That emotional connection broke through in a way the abstract arguments hadn't.

So I think it's important to be honest about this, because many of my colleagues are in the same position I was. It's not that they're bad people or that they're not smart. It's that we all have a strong incentive, psychologically and sometimes financially, to believe that what we're doing is fine. Recognizing that bias in yourself is the first step to actually looking at the evidence clearly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Bengio wanted to feel good about his life's work building AI and saw himself as one of the good guys, which made catastrophic risk concerns uncomfortable to accept.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I had a lot invested in the project of making AI smarter. I'd spent decades on it. It was my identity, it was the identity of my students, my colleagues, my whole community. So when people raised concerns about where this could lead, I didn't engage with the arguments the way I would have engaged with a scientific question. I dismissed them. Not consciously, but I'd hear the concern and I'd reach for reasons why it couldn't be a problem: it's too far away, we'll figure it out when we get there, these are not serious people.

And I now think a lot of that was motivated reasoning. When your work, your sense of purpose, your standing among your peers all depend on the belief that what you're doing is good, it's very hard to look clearly at evidence that it might be dangerous. It's like asking someone to question the foundation of their house while they're living in it.

What changed for me was partly ChatGPT, partly just sitting with the question of what happens if these systems reach human-level capability in my lifetime, maybe in my children's lifetime, and we haven't solved the problem of making sure they're aligned with us. Once I let myself actually feel that, rather than argue it away, I couldn't go back. And I felt a responsibility, because I'd contributed to getting us here.

So I try to be humble about the people who still disagree with me. I was one of them. I understand the psychology from the inside. But I'd also ask them to notice the same thing I had to notice in myself: are you reasoning, or are you defending?

r001.rationale: The candidate says his work and sense of purpose depended on believing that making AI smarter was good, which made it hard to face evidence of danger and led to motivated reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think when you’ve spent decades trying to make AI smarter, you become emotionally invested in that goal. It’s not just your work; it becomes part of your identity. You’re imagining the scientific breakthroughs, the benefits for society. So when somebody says, “Well, this could also be very dangerous,” it’s uncomfortable. Taking that seriously might mean questioning the direction of your own work.

I think that affected me. I was aware of these concerns, but I didn’t give them the attention they deserved. It was easier to think they were very far away, that we would have time to deal with them. And you don’t necessarily experience that as a bias—you feel like you’re making a reasonable judgment. That’s what makes it difficult: the emotional investment can influence which arguments you find convincing.

r001.rationale: The response says Bengio was emotionally invested in making AI smarter and found risk concerns uncomfortable, but it does not clearly identify a desire to feel good about his own work as the reason.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’ve spent your career trying to make AI smarter, you’re very invested in that goal. You believe it’s going to help people, and your work, your reputation, your sense of purpose are all connected to it. So the idea that succeeding could also create serious dangers is difficult to take in.

I think I had a tendency to find reasons why those concerns weren’t so urgent: we were still far from human intelligence, there were important things our systems couldn’t do. Those were real uncertainties, but they also made it easier to keep doing what I wanted to do. You don’t have to consciously decide to ignore a risk for that kind of bias to influence you.

And that’s uncomfortable for a scientist, because we like to think we’re guided by evidence. But we’re human beings too. We have to be willing to question not just our technical assumptions, but the motivations that make some conclusions more appealing than others.

r001.rationale: The response says Bengio was invested in making AI smarter, with his reputation and sense of purpose tied to it, and that this made risks difficult to accept and helped him find reasons to see them as less urgent. That communicates a motivation to view his work favorably.
